doc.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Wynton, the Left Bank and listening
title: Wynton Marsalis as writer and musician
summary: Heath praises Wynton's dedication, recalls his one lesson, and mentions Wynton's request for a new piece.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yeah, he was supposed to do another one himself, which is like a concert dedicated to the visual artists. If I write a piece for Picasso, or if I write a piece for Monet, or whoever they wanted be to write for… Wynton was supposed to do a mullasif and he got jammed. Wynton only took one lesson, or something. He took one lesson for me about writing and never came back. He said, “Man, you showed me so much in that one lesson,” and now I say, “Well, can I get a lesson from you?” Wynton Marsalis is writing some of the best, and he writes so much. He’s written, you know, to me, in my book I say, Wynton’s “wisdom” that’s my words for Wynton Marsalis. In my unique names, Wynton is “wisdom.” He’s so dedicated and persistent.
Oh man! Wynton Marsalis is an incredible young man to me.
He only sleeps about four hours a night.

I mean he is a super-musician. His mind set, the way he speaks, integrity, is so on it. Even John Lewis, I remember John Lewis praising Wynton, because John Lewis had an idea to marry the Western Classical music and Jazz, and that was the MJQ’s forte. But Wynton, after he won all the Grammys playing Bach, and Haydn, and all that, then he said, “Oh, no I’m not going to write that.” Except, now and then, he writes something for
a dance, Alvin Alley, or a dance troupe or something. Otherwise, he concentrates on jazz writing and he’s incredible. But, I couldn’t take him up on his offer.
